In what year did Jean Tatlock die?
Jean Tatlock: Jean Frances Tatlock (February 21, 1914 – January 4, 1944) was an American psychiatrist.
In what year was Oxycodone discovered?
Oxycodone: It is a highly addictive and commonly abused drug.
Mikoyan MiG-29: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The Mikoyan MiG-29 (Russian: Микоян МиГ-29; NATO reporting name: Fulcrum) is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.
Which company manufactures BAE Systems Hawk?
BAE Systems Hawk: Hawker Siddeley. The BAE Systems Hawk is a British single-engine, subsonic, jet-powered advanced trainer aircraft.
Who is credited with discovering Leo Minor?
Leo Minor: Johannes Hevelius. Leo Minor is a small and faint constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Graph theory?
Graph theory: Leonhard Euler. In mathematics and computer science, graph theory is the study of graphs, which are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects.
Who is credited with discovering Budesonide?
Budesonide: Ralph Brattsand. Budesonide, sold under the brand name Pulmicort, among others, is a steroid medication.
Who is credited with discovering Platinum?
Platinum: Julius Caesar Scaliger. Platinum is a chemical element; it has symbol Pt and atomic number 78.
This Swiss chemist discovered the structure of chitin in 1929 and decades later authored a memoir titled 'LSD: My Problem Child' — who was he?
Albert Hofmann (11 January 1906 - 29 April 2008) was a Swiss chemist known for being the first to synthesize, ingest, and learn of the psychedelic effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD).

Usually a symptom of coronary artery disease caused by atherosclerosis narrowing the arteries, this chest pain or pressure gets its name from Latin words meaning 'to strangle' and 'chest' — name this condition?
Angina is chest pain or pressure, usually caused by insufficient blood flow to the heart muscle (myocardium).
This general medical term describes a joint disorder in which the smooth cartilage lining wears away, leaving bone to grind directly on bone during movement — what condition is it?
Arthritis is a general medical term used to describe a disorder in which the smooth cartilagenous layer that lines a joint is lost, resulting in bone grinding on bone during joint movement.
Grown for its edible taproot in red or golden varieties and closely related to Swiss chard, this vegetable's leaves are eaten too, sold simply as "greens" — which root vegetable?
Beetroot is the taproot portion of a Beta vulgaris subsp.
In service with the U.S. Air Force since 1955 — and flown by NASA until 2007 — this subsonic strategic bomber can haul 70,000 pounds of weapons nearly 8,800 miles without refueling. Which aircraft?
Boeing B-52 Stratofortress is an American nuclear-capable subsonic jet-powered strategic bomber.
This English-like, compiled programming language was designed for business use and remains widely used today to maintain legacy mainframe systems in banking and government — what language is it?
COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
This clouding of the eye's lens is responsible for nearly 40 percent of blindness cases worldwide, often causing halos around lights and trouble seeing at night — what condition is it?
Cataract is a cloudy area in the lens of the eye that impairs vision.
Most species of this loud insect superfamily emerge annually, but a few North American ones famously emerge en masse only once every several years. What insects are they?
Cicada are a superfamily, the Cicadoidea, of insects in the order Hemiptera (true bugs).

Serving as personal doctor to a superstar singer on the day of his 2009 death, this physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter over the misuse of a surgical anesthetic as a sleep aid — who is he?
Conrad Murray (born February 19, 1953) is a Grenadian-born American former physician convicted for his role in the death of American singer and dancer Michael Jackson.

He's the only person to have won BAFTAs in black-and-white, colour, high-definition, 3D and 4K — a broadcasting career that began way back in 1954 hosting Zoo Quest. Who is this English natural historian?
David Attenborough (born 8 May 1926) is an English broadcaster, natural historian, and writer.
This Penn professor's discoveries about modified nucleosides made the Pfizer and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines possible, earning him a share of the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine — who is he?
Drew Weissman (born September 7, 1959) is an American physician and immunologist known for his contributions to RNA biology.
This Italian-American physicist won the 1938 Nobel Prize, built the world's first artificial nuclear reactor (Chicago Pile-1), and is called the "architect of the nuclear age" — who was he?

Enrico Fermi (29 September 1901 - 28 November 1954) was an Italian-American physicist, renowned for being the creator of the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, the Chicago Pile-1, and a member of the Manhattan Project.
This mutual prodrug fuses amphetamine and theophylline into one molecule, marketed as a psychostimulant and better known today as a smuggled illicit street drug — what compound is it?
Fenethylline (BAN, USAN) or fenetylline (INN) is a codrug of amphetamine and theophylline and so a mutual prodrug of both.
Home to the supermassive black hole known as Sagittarius A*, this point roughly 26,000 light-years from Earth marks the barycenter around which the Milky Way rotates — what is it?
Galactic Center is the barycenter of the Milky Way and a corresponding point on the rotational axis of the galaxy.

This American computer scientist and Navy rear admiral devised the theory of machine-independent programming languages and used it to help create COBOL, after being one of the first programmers on the Harvard Mark I — who is she?
Grace Hopper (ne Murray; December 9, 1906 - January 1, 1992) was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and United States Navy rear admiral.

Producer of Japan's first major turn-based role-playing video game, this Dutch-born American entrepreneur also secured console distribution rights to a Russian puzzle game and resolved the licensing disputes that brought it to the Game Boy — who is he?
Henk Rogers is a Dutch-born American video game designer and entrepreneur.
Often confused with a benign tumor, this cell-proliferation process increases an organ's cell count rather than the size of each cell — which term?

Hyperplasia (from Ancient Greek (hupr) 'over' and (plsis) 'formation'), or hypergenesis, is an enlargement of an organ or tissue caused by an increase in the amount of tissue that results from cell proliferation.
Whose 1687 book Principia Mathematica achieved the first great unification in physics and established classical mechanics?
This American social psychologist built 'moral foundations theory' on the idea that our moral reasoning springs from innate gut feelings rather than logic — who is he?
Jonathan Haidt (HYTE; born October 19, 1963) is an American social psychologist and author.
Home to aromatic herbs like mint, oregano, and lavender as well as the seed crop chia, this family of mostly herbaceous flowering plants is commonly known as the mints or deadnettles — which family?

Lamiaceae is a family of flowering plants commonly known as mints, deadnettles, or sages. The mint family as a whole has a cosmopolitan distribution comprising about 236 genera and around 6,900 to 7,200 species.
Equal to one cubic decimetre, this metric unit of volume was originally a base unit of the French metric system and derives its name from an old French unit of weight. What unit is it?

Litre (Commonwealth spelling) or liter (American spelling) (SI symbols L and l, other symbol used:) is a metric unit of volume. It is equal to 1 cubic decimetre (dm3), 1000 cubic centimetres (cm3) or 0.001 cubic metres (m3).
With about 6,640 living species across 27 orders — rodents and bats leading the count — this class of vertebrates feeds its young on milk. What is it?
Mammal (from Latin mamma 'breast') is a vertebrate animal of the class Mammalia.
Home to a relativistic plasma jet stretching nearly 5,000 light-years from its core, this giant elliptical galaxy sits in the constellation Virgo — which galaxy is it?
Messier 87 (also known as Virgo A or NGC 4486, generally abbreviated to M87) is a supergiant elliptical galaxy in the constellation Virgo that contains several trillion stars.
This fast-growing, drought-resistant tree native to northern India earns nicknames like 'drumstick tree' and 'horseradish tree,' and its leaves and seed pods are eaten as vegetables. What is it?
Moringa oleifera is a short-lived, fast-growing, drought-resistant tree of the family Moringaceae, native to northern India and used extensively in South and Southeast Asia.

An English aeronautical engineer who wrote novels like On the Beach and A Town Like Alice, he adopted a pen name specifically so his employers at Vickers wouldn't think him 'not a serious person.' Who is he?
Nevil Shute (17 January 1899 - 12 January 1960) was an English novelist and aeronautical engineer who spent his later years in Australia.

Physicians in this medical specialty diagnose and surgically treat eye disorders — and can often spot signs of diseases elsewhere in the body just by examining a patient's eyes — what specialty is it?
Ophthalmology is the branch of medicine that deals with the diagnosis, treatment, and surgery of eye diseases and disorders.
This British theoretical physicist, one of the founders of quantum mechanics, coined the term 'quantum electrodynamics' and shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Erwin Schrödinger — who is he?
Paul Dirac (dih-RAK; 8 August 1902 - 20 October 1984) was a British theoretical physicist who is considered to be one of the founders of quantum mechanics.
With a musty odor like freshly cut hay, this toxic colorless gas is the double acyl-chloride cousin of carbonic acid, and it saw grim use as a chemical weapon in World War I. Name the compound?
Phosgene is an organic chemical compound with the formula COCl2.
This spiny rodent actually comes in two unrelated varieties, an Old World family and a New World family, whose lookalike coats of keratin quills evolved independently — what animal is it?
Porcupine are large rodents with coats of sharp spines, or quills, that protect them against predators.

Picture benzene, but with one CH swapped for a nitrogen: this flammable, weakly alkaline liquid reeks of fish and underpins countless drugs and vitamins, churned out at 20,000 tons a year — what compound is it?
Pyridine is a basic heterocyclic organic compound with the chemical formula C5H5N.

An emeritus fellow of an Oxford college and the first-ever holder of a professorship for the public understanding of science, this British evolutionary biologist is also known as a prominent atheist author — who is he?
Richard Dawkins (born 26 March 1941) is a British evolutionary biologist, zoologist, science communicator, noted atheist, and author.

Created by Martin Odersky to address criticisms of Java, this statically typed tool blends object-oriented and functional styles, compiles to JVM bytecode, and can even transpile to JavaScript — which one?
Scala (programming language) is a strongly statically typed high-level general-purpose programming language that supports both object-oriented programming and functional programming.
This small, wingless, primitive insect takes its name from its silvery grey color and darting, fish-like movements — and its scientific name hints at a diet of sugars and starches. What is it?
Silverfish (Lepisma saccharinum) is a species of small, primitive, wingless insect in the order Zygentoma (formerly Thysanura).
This Polish-American Manhattan Project mathematician dreamed up the Monte Carlo method, the cellular automaton, and the design behind thermonuclear weapons — who was he?
Stanisław Ulam (13 April 1909 - 13 May 1984) was a Polish and, later an American mathematician who made important contributions in advancing the understanding of nuclear physics and computer science.
Its Latin species name vulgare simply means 'common,' yet this Asteraceae-family perennial turned invasive after spreading from Europe and Asia to Australia and the Americas — which plant?
Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) is a perennial, herbaceous flowering plant in the genus Tanacetum in the family Asteraceae, native to temperate Europe and Asia.
Joining a tech giant in 1998 to run worldwide operations, this executive served as its COO before stepping up to CEO the day Steve Jobs resigned in 2011 — who is he?
Tim Cook (born November 1, 1960) is an American business executive who has served as the chief executive officer (CEO) of Apple since 2011.
A byproduct of purine breakdown normally found in urine, elevated blood levels of this heterocyclic compound can cause gout and kidney stones — what's the compound (C5H4N4O3)?
Uric acid is a heterocyclic compound of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen with the formula C5H4N4O3.
Intermediate in size between the Greyhound and the Italian Greyhound, this gentle, minimal-shedding sighthound turns into a bundle of energy the moment it's outdoors — which breed?
Whippet is a British breed of sighthound. It closely resembles the Greyhound and the smaller Italian Greyhound, and is intermediate between them in size.

These ear-shaped sea snails wear a shell with a row of breathing holes and a pearly inside, and their flesh is prized as a delicacy worldwide — about 70 species, the biggest a foot long. What are they?
Abalone: Common name for a group of sea snails.
One of the world's few semiaquatic vipers, this venomous pit viper of the southeastern United States coils and displays its fangs when threatened — what is it?
A succulent from the Arabian Peninsula, this popular potted plant stores a soothing gel of acemannan in its leaves — alongside a toxic compound called aloin. What is it?
Aloe vera: Species of plant. It is widely distributed, and is considered an invasive species in many world regions.
This English mathematician earned a knighthood and the Abel Prize for proving Fermat's Last Theorem, a problem that fascinated him since childhood in Nigeria. Who is he?
Andrew Wiles: British mathematician who proved Fermat's Last Theorem.

Latin for 'worm-shaped,' this finger-like, blind-ended tube branches off the cecum and, though long considered vestigial, may actually serve as a reservoir for beneficial gut bacteria. What structure is this?
Appendix (anatomy): Tube attached to the intestine.
This ocean giant, recorded at up to 680 kg, has vanished from the Black Sea but still roams the Mediterranean and both sides of another major ocean — which fish?
Atlantic bluefin tuna: Species of fish. The Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) is a species of tuna in the family Scombridae.

Developed in the 18th century by an English clergyman and, independently, by Pierre-Simon Laplace, this rule lets you flip a conditional probability — say, finding the odds a patient is sick given a positive test. What is it?
Bayes' theorem: Mathematical rule for inverting probabilities.
Colloquially called a buffalo in the US and Canada, this large bovine is actually more closely related to yaks and cattle than to true buffalo — which animal?
This white crystalline sodium borate dissolves in water to form a basic solution and finds uses as a pesticide, a soldering flux, and an ingredient in glass and pottery glazes — what mineral is it?
Borax: Boron compound, a salt of boric acid.
This condition involves inflamed, fluid-filled sacs that normally cushion friction near joints like the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee — what is it?
Bursitis: Inflammation of the bursae (sacs of synovial fluid in joints)
Nicknamed for its heart-shaped seed pods, this mustard-family weed is considered protocarnivorous because its seeds ooze a mucilage that traps nematodes — which species?
Capsella bursa-pastoris: Species of flowering plant in the mustard family.
Which biological process oxidizes nutrients using an electron acceptor such as oxygen to generate ATP, the universal energy currency of life?
Cellular respiration: Process of releasing energy from nutrients using inorganic electron acceptors.
Discovered entirely by accident and marketed as Librium, this 1960-approved medication was the first benzodiazepine ever synthesized — what is it?
Chlordiazepoxide: Benzodiazepine medication. Chlordiazepoxide hydrochloride, sold under the brand name Librium, is a sedative and hypnotic medication of the benzodiazepine class.
Home to jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones, this phylum of aquatic invertebrates is defined by specialized stinging cells used to capture prey — what is it?
Cnidaria: Aquatic animal phylum having cnidocytes.
Better known as "pink eye," this inflammation of the clear layer over the white of the eye can leave a lid stuck shut by morning — what's the medical name?

Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the eye. Conjunctivitis, also known as pink eye, is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid.
This species includes honeydew, cantaloupe, and Casaba varieties, and traveled along ancient caravan routes long before its exact origin in the Levant or Egypt was ever confirmed — what fruit is it?
Cucumis melo: Species of plant. Cucumis melo, also known as melon or true melon, is a species of Cucumis that has been developed into many cultivated varieties.
Striking 48 to 72 hours after a heavy drinker's last drink, this potentially fatal condition brings hallucinations, seizures nicknamed 'rum fits,' and dangerously high body temperature — what is it?
Delirium tremens: Rapid onset of confusion caused by alcohol withdrawal.
The first species humans ever domesticated — over 14,000 years ago, before farming even began — this descendant of wolves later evolved to thrive on a starchy diet. What is it?
Dog: Domesticated species of canid. The dog (Canis familiaris or Canis lupus familiaris) is a domesticated descendant of wolves.
One of the Hungarian émigré scientists nicknamed the "Martians," he extended Fermi's theory of beta decay and is colloquially called the father of the hydrogen bomb — who was he?

Dubbed a 'living fossil' and commonly known as horsetail, this spore-reproducing plant genus once included 30-meter-tall trees in Carboniferous forests, its node-spacing pattern said to have inspired the invention of logarithms — which genus?

With a rich chestnut crown and a bold black patch on each white cheek, this small Old World songbird nests in cavities, walls, or abandoned magpie nests, and lays five or six eggs that hatch in under two weeks — which bird?
Eurasian tree sparrow: Species of bird. The sexes have similar plumage, and young birds are duller versions of the adult.
Born Leonardo Bonacci in Pisa, this medieval Italian mathematician's 1202 book 'Liber Abaci' introduced Europe to Indo-Arabic numerals and a famous number sequence bearing his nickname — who is he?
Dubbed the "Flying Tailor," this inventor was so sure his wearable parachute would work that he leapt from the Eiffel Tower to test it himself — fatally. Who was he?
Dubbed "the Godfather of AI" for his pioneering work on neural networks, this Nobel laureate quit Google in 2023 to warn about AI's risks. Who is he?
Google's web mapping platform offers satellite imagery, live traffic and route planning, plus 360-degree interactive panoramas taken along roads. What is that panorama feature called?
Google Maps offers satellite imagery, aerial photography, street maps, 360-degree interactive panoramic views of streets known as Street View, real-time traffic conditions and route planning.
An HTTP 404 is proof that which part of the process actually worked?
404 means the browser reached the server perfectly well and the server could not supply the resource. A server you cannot reach at all gives you a different error entirely.
This inflammation of the liver can cause jaundice and, if it becomes chronic, progress to cirrhosis — most commonly caused by five different viruses labeled A through E. What condition is it?
Hepatitis: Inflammation of the liver. Hepatitis is acute if it resolves within six months, and chronic if it lasts longer than six months.
The most widespread of all primates, this bipedal, nearly hairless species owes its advanced technology, culture, and language to a large, complex brain — what is it?
Human: Species of hominid in the genus Homo.
Typically starting to work within an hour, this NSAID relieves pain, fever, and inflammation but can worsen asthma and, in later pregnancy, is considered harmful — which drug?

A theoretical physicist who studied under Max Born earned a chemistry degree from Harvard before pivoting to nuclear physics — and later oversaw the first atomic weapons during WWII. Who is this pivotal figure in physics history?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: American theoretical physicist (1904–1967)

The id Software programmer behind Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, and Quake later left to become CTO of Oculus VR — before walking away again to chase artificial general intelligence. Which 3D-graphics wizard is he?
John Carmack: American computer programmer and video game developer (born 1970)
Defined by a carbon-oxygen double bond flanked by two carbon groups, this class of organic compound includes acetone and gives some sugars and steroids like testosterone their structure — what is it?
Ketone: Organic compounds of the form >C=O.

This trigonometric relationship links each side of a triangle to the angle across from it, with every such ratio equal to twice the radius of the triangle's circumscribed circle. What is the rule called?
Law of sines: Property of all triangles on a Euclidean plane.
Named in honor of a pioneer of sterile surgery, this genus of bacteria causes a rare but serious foodborne illness with a fatality rate up to 30 percent — what is it?
Listeria: Genus of bacteria. Listeria is a genus of bacteria that acts as an intracellular parasite in mammals.
Encoded by the codons AAA and AAG, this basic, essential amino acid cannot be synthesized by the human body — which one is it?
Lysine: Amino acid. Lysine (symbol Lys or K) is an α-amino acid that is a precursor to many proteins.
A Russian pediatric endocrinologist also known by the surname Faassen, this woman is the elder child of Russia's president. Who is she?
Maria Vorontsova: Daughter of Vladimir Putin (born 1985)
This waxy crystalline compound from peppermint and corn mint produces a cooling sensation when inhaled or rubbed on skin, and brings local-anesthetic relief to a sore throat — what is it?
Menthol: Organic compound used as flavouring and analgesic.
Soviet pilots nicknamed this 1972 gunship the 'flying tank,' a helicopter NATO calls 'Hind' that can also haul eight troops and still flies in 52 countries. What is it?
Mil Mi-24: Family of assault and attack helicopters.

Synthesized in 2003 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna and named in 2016 for the Russian region around it, this element 115 has a most-stable isotope lasting just 0.65 seconds — what is it?
Moscovium: Chemical element with atomic number 115 (Mc)

As modern science emerged, this concept came to mean the passive reality moved by divine laws — and after the Industrial Revolution, the part of the world untouched by intentional human hands. What word is it?
Nature: Material world and its phenomena.
Born in New York to Holocaust-survivor parents, this political scientist made the politics of the Holocaust and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict his life's work. Who is he?
Colloquially called harvestmen or daddy long legs, this arachnid order looks startlingly modern in 400-million-year-old fossils from Scotland's Rhynie cherts — what is it?
Opiliones: Order of arachnids. The Opiliones (formerly Phalangida) are an order of arachnids, colloquially known as harvestmen, harvesters, daddy long legs, or granddaddy long legs.

Sold over the counter under brand names like Tylenol and Panadol, this analgesic eases mild migraines and tension headaches but is famously inferior to ibuprofen at knocking down a fever — what is it?
Paracetamol: Medication for pain and fever.
This nerve-damage condition can be triggered by diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, or certain chemotherapy and antibiotic drugs, and may come on suddenly or creep in slowly — what is it?
Peripheral neuropathy: Nervous system disease affecting nerves beyond the brain and spinal cord.
This Dutch experimental physicist shared the 1902 Nobel Prize with Hendrik Lorentz for discovering and explaining an effect that now bears his name — who was he?
Covered in sharp keratin quills for defense, this rodent's largest species ranks as the third-biggest living rodent in the world, behind only the capybara and the beaver. What animal is it?
Porcupine: Rodent with a coat of sharp spines.
Nicknamed 'gold cap' and 'golden halo,' this is the world's best-known psilocybin-containing mushroom thanks to its wide distribution and how easily it's cultivated — which species?
Psilocybe cubensis: Species of fungus. It belongs to the fungus family Hymenogastraceae and was previously known as Stropharia cubensis.
Also known as steelhead in its sea-run form, this North American Pacific species shows off a vivid reddish stripe along its flank in breeding males — which fish?
Rainbow trout: Fresh-water species of fish.
His 'Essai Sur La Nature Du Commerce' was called the 'cradle of political economy'; this Irish-French banker made a fortune speculating in John Law's Mississippi Company — who is it?
Richard Cantillon: Irish-French economist and banker (c. 1680 – 1734)
This light Swedish single-engine supersonic fighter has a delta wing and canard configuration with fly-by-wire controls and is fully NATO interoperable — what is it?
Saab JAS 39 Gripen: Light single-engined multirole fighter aircraft from Sweden.
Living on ocean floors worldwide, this leathery-skinned echinoderm recycles nutrients as a detritivore and is named for its resemblance to a common garden vegetable — what is it?

Composed of repeating siloxane units with a backbone of oxygen and silicon rather than carbon, this synthetic material fills sealants, cookware, and medical devices, and is often confused with the chip-making element it's named after — what is it?

Introduced in Einstein's 1905 paper 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies,' this theory rests on two postulates — that physical laws hold in every non-accelerating frame, and that light's speed is constant for all observers. What is it called?
Special relativity: Theory of interwoven space and time by Albert Einstein.

Named from Greek words meaning 'a chain of berries' and 'pus-forming,' this Gram-positive bacterial species is the predominant carrier of the Lancefield group A antigen, often abbreviated GAS — what is this bacterium's full scientific name?
Streptococcus pyogenes: Species of bacterium. The name group A (beta-hemolytic) Streptococcus is thus also used.
This orange citrus fruit is usually considered a mandarin variety, though it's also thought to carry some pomelo ancestry — which fruit?

Born from 19th-century efforts to make steam engines more efficient — thanks largely to French physicist Sadi Carnot — this branch of physics is governed by four fundamental laws relating heat, work, and energy. What is it?

Thermodynamics: Physics of heat, work, and temperature. The initial application of thermodynamics to mechanical heat engines was quickly extended to the study of chemical compounds and chemical reactions.

Once dismissed as rare and bizarre, this childhood-onset disorder pairs multiple motor tics with at least one vocal tic, often heralded by a premonitory urge the person can briefly suppress — what's it called?
Tourette syndrome: Neurodevelopmental disorder involving motor and vocal tics.
Often caused by poor circulation or prolonged pressure on the skin, this open sore — also known as a bedsore when linked to immobility — can destroy tissue down to the fat layer. What is it called?

First glimpsed through Dmitri Ivanovsky's 1892 study of an ailing tobacco plant, this is the most numerous biological entity on Earth — yet it can only replicate inside another organism's living cells. What is it?
Virus: Infectious agent that replicates in cells.
This American child prodigy entered Harvard at 11 and lectured on four-dimensional geometry at 12 before deliberately retreating from public life — who was he?
William James Sidis: American mathematician, polyglot, and child prodigy (1898–1944)
Iron is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for iron is Fe. Iron is a chemical element; it has symbol Fe and atomic number 26.
Plutonium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for plutonium is Pu. Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.

In what year was Salma Hayek born?
Salma Hayek: Salma Valgarma Hayek Pinault ( HY-ek, Spanish: [ˈsalma ˈxaʝek]; née Hayek Jiménez; born September 2, 1966) is a Mexican and American actress and film producer.
In what year was Meg Ryan born?
Meg Ryan: Margaret Mary Emily Anne Hyra (born November 19, 1961), known professionally as Meg Ryan, is an American actress.
In what year was Christina Applegate born?
Christina Applegate (born November 25, 1971) is a retired American actress.
In what year was Tom Hardy born?
Tom Hardy: Edward Thomas Hardy (born 15 September 1977) is an English actor.
In what year was Karen Gillan born?
Karen Gillan: Karen Sheila Gillan (born 28 November 1987) is a Scottish actress and filmmaker.

Sridevi: Sridevi's career spanned over 50 years in a wide range of genres.

Jonathan Majors: Jonathan Michael Majors (born September 7, 1989) is an American actor.
In what year was Jack Nicholson born?
Jack Nicholson: John Joseph Nicholson (born April 22, 1937) is an American retired actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Poonam Pandey born?
Poonam Pandey (born 11 March 1991) is an Indian media personality and actress.
In what year was Vanessa Kirby born?
Vanessa Kirby: Vanessa Nuala Kirby (born 18 April 1987 or 1988) is an English actress.
In what year was Jamie Dornan born?
Jamie Dornan: James Peter Maxwell Dornan (born 1 May 1982) is an actor, model, and musician from Northern Ireland.
In what year did David McCallum die?
David McCallum: David Keith McCallum (19 September 1933 – 25 September 2023) was a Scottish actor and musician.
In what year was The Fallout first released?
The Fallout is a 2021 American drama film written and directed by Megan Park in her feature film directorial debut.
In what year was The Untouchables first released?
The Untouchables is a 1987 American crime film directed by Brian De Palma, produced by Art Linson and written by David Mamet.
In what year was Knock at the Cabin first released?
Knock at the Cabin is a 2023 American apocalyptic psychological horror film co-written, directed and produced by M.
In what year was Priscilla first released?
Priscilla (film): It follows the life of Priscilla (Cailee Spaeny) and her complicated romantic relationship with Elvis Presley (Jacob Elordi).
In what year was Bawaal first released?
